tip: Του Αγίου (tu ayíu) = of the Saint – Greek names a feast day with the of-form: του Αγίου Δημητρίου (tu ayíu Dhimitríu) = St Demetrius's day.
Να (na) before a verb turns it into a wish: να χαίρεσαι (na khérese) = may you enjoy it, the standard add-on to a name day greeting.
The celebrant treats everyone: όποιος γιορτάζει (ópios yortázi = whoever celebrates) φέρνει γλυκά (férni ghliká = brings sweets) – the reverse of the usual birthday setup.
Του χρόνου (tu khrónu) is literally 'of the year' and means next year: και του χρόνου! (ke tu khrónu) wishes the same happy day comes round again.
Καλή Ανάσταση (kalí Anástasi) = the wish before Easter night.
Μεγάλη Παρασκευή (Megháli Paraskeví) is literally 'Great Friday' – a mourning day with the year's strictest fast, which is why κρέας (kréas = meat) is off the table.
Χριστός Ανέστη (Khristós Anésti) keeps the old verb form ανέστη (anésti) = he rose; today's Greek would say αναστήθηκε (anastíthike).
Αληθώς Ανέστη (Alithós Anésti = truly He is risen) is the fixed reply to the Easter greeting Χριστός Ανέστη (Khristós Anésti) – a set call-and-response, not a free choice of words.
Τον Απρίλιο (ton Aprílio) = in April – Greek drops the word for in and lets the article τον (ton) mark the time: έπεσε τον Απρίλιο (épese ton Aprílio) = it fell in April.
Christmas is plural in Greek: τα Χριστούγεννα (ta Khristúyena) takes the plural article τα (ta), and words with it go plural too: καλά Χριστούγεννα (kalá Khristúyena) = merry Christmas.
Στόλιζαν (stólizan) = they used to decorate – the ongoing past form, for what people did year after year.
Μελομακάρονα (melomakárona, honey cookies) vs κουραμπιέδες (kurabiédhes, sugared almond ones) splits most Greek households at Christmas – people usually have a firm favourite.
The -άκια (-ákia) ending shrinks things fondly: φώτα (fóta = lights) becomes φωτάκια (fotákia) = the little Christmas lights.
Ο Άι-Βασίλης (o Ái-Vasílis) is St Basil, not St Nicholas – his feast is Jan 1, so gifts traditionally arrive την Πρωτοχρονιά (tin Protokhroniá = on New Year's Day), not at Christmas.
Το πρώτο κομμάτι (to próto komáti = the first slice) of the New Year cake usually follows a set order: Christ, then the house, then anyone absent, then everyone by age.
Σου εύχομαι (su éfkhome) = I wish you – the little word σου (su) covers to you on its own, so Greek needs no word for to.
Όποιος πιάσει (ópios piási) = whoever catches – for a single future grab Greek uses the one-off form πιάσει, not the everyday πιάνει (piáni).
Η Τσικνοπέμπτη (i Tsiknopémpti) = 'Smoky Thursday', a day of grilled meat.
Απόκριες (Apókries = Carnival) turns into a describing word with -ιάτικο: αποκριάτικο πάρτι (apokriátiko párti) = a carnival party.
Σαρακοστή (Sarakostí = Lent) comes from σαράντα (saránda = forty) – the name counts the 40 days that Καθαρά Δευτέρα (Kathará Dheftéra = Clean Monday) opens.
The Lenten fast bans animals with blood, so θαλασσινά (thalasiná = seafood like shellfish) and ελιές (eliés = olives) pass while meat and dairy don't.
Πετούσαμε (petúsame) = we were flying – the ongoing past form, for something that ran on all afternoon.
Παίρνω τηλέφωνο (pérno tiléfono) = to call – literally 'I take phone', so πάρε με τηλέφωνο (páre me tiléfono) = call me.
Χτυπάει (khtipái) = it's ringing – the verb literally means it knocks, which is what Greek phones and doorbells do.
The ξανα- (ksana-) prefix means again: θα σε ξαναπάρω (tha se ksanapáro) = I'll call you again, i.e. call you back. It glues onto most verbs.
Κλείνω το τηλέφωνο (klíno to tiléfono) = hang up, literally 'I close the phone'; telling someone to do it is κλείσε (klíse).
Μη με παίρνεις (mi me pérnis) = don't call me – the ongoing verb form after μη (mi) makes it a standing rule, not just this once.
Νούμερό σου (número su) takes a second accent: a word stressed three syllables from the end adds one when σου (su) or μου (mu) is tacked on.
Μιλάει (milái) = he's talking, but of a phone it means the line is busy: μιλάει συνέχεια (milái sinékhia) = it's engaged non-stop.
A plain present question does the work of a polite request: μου στέλνεις; (mu stélnis) = could you send me?
